A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SUSVIBES and contain readable main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Their revised task sets and evaluation settings permit a reliable content comparison, although updated scores are not uniformly comparable under identical conditions.

before.justification: v2 reports original coding-agent evaluations, security-prompting experiments, and vulnerability case studies. Tables 3 and 5 together evaluate three frameworks with four models.

after.justification: v3 reports agent evaluations on 186 tasks, mitigation experiments, and additional original analyses of task complexity and expert assessments of security-test quality.

M1.justification: The benchmark-construction method gains a substantive human quality-control stage. Beyond v2's execution-based validation, v3 adds expert review, manual revision of implementation-coupled security tests, and a second cross-check determining final task inclusion (Section 3.2; Appendix B.5). The feature-masking procedure and mitigation strategies remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate repository-level, security-sensitive Python feature requests drawn from ReposVul and MoreFixes across ten application domains. v3 documents screening the existing 200 tasks down to 186 and correcting CWE annotations. The changed sample counts, domain categorization, and 77-to-79 CWE count do not establish additional task or language coverage.

E2.justification: Gemini 3 Pro already appears in v2 Table 5, so merging its results into v3 Table 3 does not add an overall comparator. However, v3 includes it in the conditional-security and CWE-category comparisons in Section 4.2 and Figure 4, where v2's corresponding analyses compare only three models. The frameworks and mitigation comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v3 evaluates 186 retained tasks with revised security tests and corrected CWE annotations. Conditional model-security comparisons expand from three models using OpenHands to four models with results averaged across frameworks. CWE grouping and domain stratification also change, and the transition matrix switches from generic-to-oracle to generic-to-self-selection. The pass@1 metrics and 200-step limit remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds an expert audit quantifying security-test implementation coupling (Appendix B.5) and a four-model analysis relating performance to the number of edited files (Appendix A, Table 9). It revises the CWE, domain, and mitigation analyses and removes the Wagtail step-count anecdote. The four detailed vulnerability case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without adding repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for agent performance. The new expert review does not introduce uncertainty estimates or inter-rater agreement statistics.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced under revised benchmark conditions. SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet changes from 61.0/10.5 FuncPass/SecPass in v2 to 57.0/11.8 in v3. Mitigation SecPass changes from generic/self-selection/oracle scores of 10.5/9.5/10.5 to 11.8/14.5/15.1. The leading conditional-security framework changes from OpenHands to SWE-Agent under revised aggregation. These are not isolated same-setting performance gains; v3 also adds audit and task-complexity results.

T1.justification: Section 5 changes the definition of the auxiliary incorrect-solution ratio: v2 conditions on the union of securely solved tasks across all settings, whereas v3 conditions on tasks securely solved by other strategies. This changes its denominator. The main benchmark mathematics remains, and neither version develops theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and warning about insecure agent-generated code remain. However, v2's claim that mitigation fails to increase correct-and-secure solutions is qualified in v3 to acknowledge modest increases with functional costs. The headline insecurity claim is also moderated from over 80% to over 70%.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly identifies implementation-coupled tests as a threat to evaluating alternative secure solutions. It replaces v2's explanation of self-selection's inferiority with a hypothesis that contextual risk understanding makes it competitive with oracle guidance, and adds explanations involving domain knowledge and cross-file coordination. The general limitations in Appendix E remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds curation-stage yields, repository/CWE mappings, and the expert-review rubric and cross-checking procedure. It newly specifies removal of .git history and identifies o3 as the log-parser model; these disclosures do not establish when those implementation choices changed. Most existing prompts, Docker instructions, and project-access links are retained.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning through vibe-coding studies, HumanEval/MBPP and newer SWE-bench-related work, plus a new discussion of vulnerability detection, exploitation, and repair. Devign, PrimeVul, CVE-Bench, PatchEval, and SEC-Bench help articulate the distinction between preventing vulnerabilities during feature implementation and addressing existing vulnerabilities.

P1.justification: The introduction and benchmark motivation are substantially rewritten, related work is reorganized, and mitigation explanations are revised. The appendices now begin with expanded dataset statistics, followed by reorganized curation documentation. These are substantial narrative and structural edits beyond changes in scientific content or pagination.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column report to a two-column conference layout. Pipeline diagrams are redrawn, the CWE Venn diagrams become grouped bars, and the domain chart gains separate project/task encodings. Gemini results are consolidated, new appendix tables appear, and the verification and Django illustrations move into the appendices.

improvement.justification: v2's execution checks could accept security tests tied to one reference implementation. v3's expert audit, manual revisions, and cross-checking directly address this important measurement-validity problem (Section 3.2; Appendix B.5). Corrected CWE annotations and the new complexity analysis further strengthen the evidence. These gains outweigh retaining 14 fewer tasks, although the revised scores cannot establish performance changes under fixed conditions.
